articles.title: South East businesses speak about the impact of retail crime
articles.summary: Businesses reveal the impact of shoplifting with recorded offences still above pre-pandemic levels.
articles.body:
A shop owner has described how she locks her door during opening hours and customers have to ring the bell to get in after her store was targeted by thieves last year.

Paige Mengers, who runs a designer boutique in Surrey, has been speaking about the impact of shoplifting, with recorded offences remaining above pre-pandemic levels.

Home Office figures show there were 42,674 shoplifting offences across Kent, Surrey and Sussex in 2025/26 compared with 28,048 cases in 2019/20.

The government said overall offences in England and Wales fell 4% last year, with more suspects being charged.

Mengers, who has stores in Cobham and south-west London, said she boosted security after a raid in January 2025 involving men with wire cutters.

"One barricaded the door, the other came in and cut the wires on the bags and stole quite a lot of them," she said.

"It was absolutely awful, I lost two very good members of staff who were terrified after that.

"We were really shaken and for about six months I had security on the doors for our staff."

The borough commander for Elmbridge Chris Thoday told BBC South East the tactics used by these groups were "pretty sophisticated".

"They're very organised, they know exactly what they are doing," he said.

"Quite often they will recce the shops beforehand, then go in afterwards, steal the items they want to take, to make sure they're in and out as quickly as possible."

Insp Thoday said a number of stores had since trialled the use of lone worker alarms for staff working alone at night in a number of shops in Cobham.

Official data shows 23 per cent of investigations across England and Wales led to a charge or summons in the 12 months up to April this year.

It's not just high street stores being targeted, rural areas are also affected.

Bosses at a family-run farm shop in Wingham, near Canterbury in Kent, said they had suffered thousands of pounds of losses in a year.

"We're getting small gangs come in or individuals to steal high value goods, either meat products, meat joints or alcohol," said Andrew Gibson, director at Gibson's Farm Shop.

"They seem to be more organised, out here you have to drive here, you can't be an opportunist thief."

Gibson recently turned to social media to shame offenders online.

"We've had the situation where thieves have gone back into a police station with the money for the goods to pay back to us," he said.

In Canterbury, Kent Police have set up a dedicated retail crime team.

"People are going in, stealing to order, filling up trolleys and just running out of the stores," said James, a plain clothed police officer speaking to BBC South East during an operation to catch thieves.

He said crime groups would sometimes scope out stores and film items they wanted stolen, before sending shoplifters in.

"We notice people coming in checking out where the CCTV cameras are," he said.

"Sometimes a shoplifter will use trolleys, they'll load up what they want to take and then they'll hover by the entrance or exit and when the opportunity comes they just take the whole trolley load of goods.

"We've also noticed people with prams loading up the bottom or the top, wandering around pretending they are getting something out for the young child in the pram and then load up the pram and take items out of the store."

Paul Stoner, district commander for police in the city, said the team was set up as a response to a rise in crime over an 18-month period.

"It's a set few individuals who commit a disproportionate amount of that crime," he said.

"Our officers have a really good knowledge of the local offenders, we are able to identify them very quickly through the CCTV images," he said.

"What we also have is the ability to put those images through facial recognition, if the suspect is on a database, we're able to identify them."

Police also share information with the local City Watch scheme and details about known suspects can be relayed on a radio system to shops.

It's run by the Canterbury Business Improvement District (Bid) and links up retailers with the police and the city council's CCTV control centre.

Lisa Carlson, chief executive of Canterbury Bid, said they had a street team which trained businesses, helping them gather and submit evidence.

"We have 137 radios in circulation, if there is an incident unfolding it can be reported in real time and hopefully we can avoid any crime happening," she said.

In Sussex, the Brighton and Hove Business Crime Reduction Partnership (BCRP) also provides services to fight crime and anti-social behaviour.

They are working with other BCRPs around Sussex to identify repeat offenders, according to manager Lisa Perretta.

"When someone becomes quite well-known in one area, it will be flagged to our area, so we are forewarned and can identify them a lot earlier before they commit multiple crimes," she said.

Perretta said they had also got a lot better at educating businesses to report crime.

Recorded shoplifting offences across the South East peaked in 2024/25.

Only Kent saw an increase in cases over the last 12 months with reductions in Surrey and Sussex.

Olivia Carroll, temporary chief inspector at Sussex Police, said there was a "large number of reports" of retail crime in the county - including "organised criminality" by groups.

"Clearly we deal with repeat prolific offenders and our focus is on that as a priority," she said.

A Home Office spokesperson said retail crime had been "dismissed as low-level offending" but it harmed shopworkers and damaged businesses.

"Shop theft is down 4% on last year and charges are up 19%," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: 'H-1B visas should not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners': JD Vance
articles.summary: US News: US Vice President JD Vance has defended the Trump administration’s efforts to reform the H-1B visa programme, saying the system should \"not exist to r.
articles.body: US Vice President JD Vance has defended the Trump administration’s efforts to reform the H-1B visa programme, saying the system should "not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners."Speaking on the business and technology show All-In Podcast, Vance said the administration pursued changes through executive and administrative measures because of the lack of political support in Congress for legislative reform.“Look, man, we looked at the fraud in the system and we said, you know, one, Congress is not going to pass a law changing this. There just isn't the political will to do it. So what are the things that we can do administratively to ensure that if a tech company is going to try to get an H-1B visa, it's an actual genius,” Vance said.He further said that the programme should focus on workers who can make a substantial contribution to the technology sector and the wider US economy.“It's a person that is going to significantly enrich the tech ecosystem or the American economy. You know, you're not just replacing one accountant who makes $60,000 with a lower-wage foreign accountant who makes $45,000 a year. That is not what the programme exists for,” he added.Vance also highlighted a $100,000 fee introduced by the administration and said officials were examining measures to prevent companies from using H-1B workers while simultaneously laying off American employees.“And so we came up with this idea to impose this $100,000 fee. We're also looking at various ways of preventing companies that use H-1B visas from laying off a bunch of American workers. So you know, one of the things that I find just shocking about this is you'll have a company that applies for an H-1B and they'll say, oh, we're desperate for workers.”He questioned companies that claim they cannot find workers despite having recently carried out large-scale layoffs. “We can't find the workers. And then you go and look at their history and they've laid off 5,000 people. Well, that's ridiculous.”Vance said companies that lay off US workers should not then turn to foreign workers to fill similar positions.“If you're laying off American workers, you shouldn't be going to the market searching for foreign workers to replace them. So we're doing a lot within the confines, of course, of what we're allowed to do legally. We've gotten sued on some of this stuff, but I think fundamentally we're on the right on both the law and the policy,” he added.Reiterating the administration’s stated objective for the H-1B programme, Vance said, “The H-1B should not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners. It should exist to enrich the American economy. And that's exactly what we're trying to make sure it does.”Vance was raised in Middletown, Ohio, and spent summers with extended family in Jackson, Kentucky. His upbringing in Ohio and Appalachia has played a significant role in shaping his political identity.The UP president is married to Usha Chilukuri Vance, an Indian-origin lawyer and former litigator. The couple met at Yale Law School and married in 2014. They have four children.

articles.title: In 2020, 11 sheep in Brazil ignored ordinary shade cloth and spent 38% of their time beneath solar panels, even though both shelters blocked sunlight
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A recent Brazilian study found that 11 sheep spent 38% of their time under solar panels compared to less than 1% under conventional shade cloth, suggesting solar panels may serve dual purposes in agriculture.
articles.body: Five Corriedale lambs and six Corriedale ewes were given a choice between two shelters in a Brazilian experiment; one covered with photovoltaic panels and another made from cloth that was designed to block 80% of sunlight. The sheep barely used the cloth shelter, and spent 38% of their observed time beneath the solar panels. The experiment was conducted at the Animal Biometeorology Laboratory of São Paulo State University in Jaboticabal, Brazil. Researchers watched the 11 animals over five days, and recorded their behavior at 10-minute intervals from morning till late afternoon.The animals had access to both forms of shade as well as direct sunlight, and their behavior was recorded across activities including grazing, ruminating, standing, lying and spending time under each shelter. The results were published in the Journal of Cleaner Production in 2020, where the researchers reported that the sheep spent less than 1% of their time under the 80%-blockage cloth but 38% under the photovoltaic panels, with the remaining 61% spent exposed to the sun. The researchers measured environmental conditions under both shelters and found that the solar-panel shade reduced radiant heat load by about 40 watts per square metre when compared with the cloth shade.The two shelters blocked sunlight differentlyThe experiment was designed around a practical question in agrivoltaics, which was whether solar panels could serve two purposes on farmland and produce electricity while also providing usable shade for livestock. The U.S. Department of Energy defines agrivoltaics as the co-location of agriculture and solar energy, which includes livestock grazing beneath or between rows of photovoltaic panels. The agency notes that solar arrays can alter the microclimate underneath them, with daytime temperatures often cooler under the panels. Sheep are already being used for grazing at solar facilities in the United States and Europe.The sheep could choose between photovoltaic shade and a conventional artificial shelter, which matters because both structures were designed to reduce direct solar radiation. The panel structure nevertheless created a different environment, where the researchers recorded solar radiation, air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and black-globe temperature in the shaded and exposed areas.As sunlight intensified, the animals increasingly moved away from direct exposure and toward the panel shade. The proportion of time spent outside the shelters fell from about 96.7% to 30.2% when solar radiation increased from 250 to 850 watts per square metre, and time spent under the photovoltaic panels rose from about 13% to 69.3%.The panels were producing electricity while providing shadeThe experiment also measured the energy produced by the photovoltaic system, and found that electricity generation, as well as solar radiation, increased. The researchers calculated that the system generated about 5.19 megawatt-hours of electricity over a year, based on their measurements and assumptions. They estimated that this would correspond to about 2.77 tonnes of avoided carbon dioxide emissions and roughly $740 in annual electricity savings under the conditions used in their analysis. Those figures came from the study's specific experimental and economic assumptions rather than from a full-scale commercial solar farm.The sheep study was small, involving only 11 animals, so its findings cannot by themselves establish that all sheep will prefer photovoltaic shade, and the researchers described it as an investigation of shade preference and radiant heat load, not a large livestock-production trial. A study published in Small Ruminant Research found that nine Corriedale ewes exposed to solar-panel shade experienced lower radiant heat load and reductions in wool-surface and skin temperatures while using the shade during periods of high solar radiation. The 2020 experiment had already shown that the sheep were not treating the two shelters as equivalent, and given a choice, they spent almost no time under the cloth and considerably more beneath the photovoltaic panels. The reason identified by the researchers was not that the animals could somehow detect electricity; their shade produced by the panel reduced the radiant heat reaching the animals, which made that space more attractive during periods of stronger solar radiation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A teenager who survived childhood cancer started collecting LEGO for the hospital that treated him; his drive has now donated 573 mini-figures and raised $2,575
articles.summary: US News: Sometimes a small act of kindness goes so far that it touches your heart for an entire lifetime. Alexander Ackled-Dold still remembers the little thin.
articles.body: Sometimes a small act of kindness goes so far that it touches your heart for an entire lifetime. Alexander Ackled-Dold still remembers the little things when he was receiving treatment for leukaemia as a child at Southlake's pediatric oncology clinic. The teen recounted how the staff were always kind as he was in and out of hospitals for treatment, they drew smiley faces on his bandages and one volunteer even provided LEGO minifigures to the children whenever they came in for treatment.Now in Grade 12 and cancer-free, he said those actions have made a lifetime of difference and inspired him to do the same for others going through treatment today. “Whenever I would go, I just remembered the little things some of the nurses would do that would make the visit less about me going there to get a treatment,” he said.Thus, Alexander and his family launched the Southlake Superheroes donation drive in September. The campaign sought donations of LEGO figures and cash to donate to Southlake's pediatric oncology clinic. So far, the initiative has donated 573 mini-figures and raised more than $2,575 to help provide new LEGO sets.His father, Simon Ackles-Dold, said the initiative has gone well so far, with the children loving the little figures by all counts. "There was good initial feedback, positive feedback," he said. “A lot of the younger kids at Alex’s school were donating their old LEGO figures, so lots of teenagers were giving, which is really nice to see.”The project aims to give kids something fun to look forward to when they receive treatment, akin to what Alexander experienced when he was younger and in that situation. “It’s a good distraction for the kids when they’re there,” Ackles-Dold said.While the campaign does not donate to the children directly, since access is limited during treatment, Alexander said it was great interacting with staff there again, years after he was a patient. “It’s been a long time, and it’s been nice to give back to them and see them all happy about what I’m doing,” he said.The family hopes to be able to grow the effort and continue fundraising in the coming months. They are still collecting cash donations or donations of LEGO figures, though old LEGO sets are disallowed because of the need to sterilise whatever they donate.Interested individuals can donate by contacting the Southlake Heroes Instagram page or GoFundMe page.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, a New Orleans project began crushing bottles into sand; six years later, it has diverted 12 million pounds of glass to help rebuild shrinking coastal wetlands
articles.summary: US News: A bottle tossed away in New Orleans does not necessarily have to end its life in a landfill. A project launched in 2020 is giving discarded glass a se.
articles.body: A bottle tossed away in New Orleans does not necessarily have to end its life in a landfill. A project launched in 2020 is giving discarded glass a second purpose; crushing bottles into sand that can be used in coastal restoration. Glass Half Full, founded by Tulane University students Franziska Trautmann and Max Steitz, has grown from a small backyard operation into a larger recycling programme. In February 2026, Tulane University reported that the initiative had diverted more than 12 million pounds of glass from landfills. The project is now turning a common waste stream into material that can support efforts to restore Louisiana’s vulnerable coastline.From discarded bottles to recycled sandThe idea behind Glass Half Full is relatively simple: collect unwanted glass, crush it and give the resulting material a new use. The organisation accepts glass through residential and commercial pickups as well as drop-off programmes before processing it at its facility. According to Tulane University, the operation can process about two tons of glass per hour, turning the waste into sand and gravel for several industries, with coastal restoration being a major focus.That approach grew from the founders’ frustration with the lack of glass recycling infrastructure in New Orleans. When Trautmann and Steitz started the initiative in 2020, they used a small machine and a grassroots collection model. Community support helped the project expand, eventually moving from its early backyard setup to a larger recycling operation capable of handling much greater volumes. The recycled material now has applications beyond coastal work. Glass Half Full produces sand and gravel that can be used in construction, disaster relief and other projects, while the organisation continues to develop its coastal restoration programme.Why recycled glass matters for Louisiana’s coastLouisiana’s coastline faces persistent land loss, making the search for restoration materials an important part of efforts to rebuild vulnerable wetlands. Traditional restoration projects can rely on sediment dredged from the Mississippi River, but researchers are examining whether recycled glass could supplement those materials. In April 2026, Tulane researchers described an ongoing experiment involving four constructed islands in wetlands east of New Orleans. Two sets of islands are being compared; one uses dredged river sand, while the other combines river sand with recycled glass sand produced by Glass Half Full. Researchers are studying how vegetation develops on the different surfaces over time.The experiment reflects a broader research effort known as ReCoast, which brings together scientists from fields including ecology, engineering and coastal science. The programme is investigating how recycled glass sand can be used safely and effectively in coastal restoration, including how plants respond to the material and where it may be most useful.Testing whether glass can help rebuild wetlandsThe concept is not simply to replace natural coastal sediment with crushed bottles. Researchers are studying how glass sand can work alongside other materials and biological systems. Recent Tulane research has focused on growing coastal cypress and other plants in recycled glass sand. Researchers found that some wetland plants do not grow well in glass sand alone, leading them to examine mixtures containing nutrient-rich Mississippi River sediment as well as beneficial bacteria and fungi. The aim is to create conditions in which plants can establish themselves and eventually help stabilise newly restored areas. That plant growth is important because restoration is about more than adding material to an eroded shoreline. Once vegetation becomes established, roots can help hold sediment together and create habitat, allowing newly constructed areas to develop into functioning wetland ecosystems.Glass Half Full has already worked with Tulane researchers and other partners on restoration projects. The collaboration has included projects in southeast Louisiana, including work at Big Branch Marsh National Wildlife Refuge and with the Pointe-au-Chien Tribe in areas affected by Hurricane Ida.Turning a waste problem into a restoration resourceThe project’s growth illustrates how a material traditionally treated as waste can be redirected towards a local environmental need. Instead of discarded bottles travelling to a landfill, they can be collected, processed and transformed into a material that researchers are testing for use in wetlands and other restoration projects. The scale has also changed considerably since 2020. Tulane University reported that Glass Half Full has now diverted more than 12 million pounds of glass from landfills, while the organisation continues to process millions of pounds each year. The work does not mean recycled glass can replace every source of sediment or solve Louisiana’s coastal land-loss challenges on its own. Instead, researchers are testing where the material can be useful, how it should be mixed with natural sediment and which plants can establish successfully in it.For New Orleans, however, the premise remains strikingly direct: bottles that once represented a waste problem can be transformed into sand and put back to work. Six years after Glass Half Full began, its millions of pounds of diverted glass are becoming part of a much larger experiment in turning everyday waste into a resource for Louisiana’s changing coastline.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2005, New York buried 1.1 million scrap tyres beneath I-87 near Plattsburgh; the discarded rubber helped replace two ageing bridges with a highway
articles.summary: US News: In a groundbreaking highway project, New York State utilized 1.1 million scrap tyres as alternative fill beneath I-87, transforming waste into infrastructure while replacing obsolete bridges over an abandoned railroad.
articles.body: About 1.1 million discarded passenger tyres ended up beneath Interstate 87 south of Plattsburgh, New York inside an engineered embankment built after two ageing bridges over an abandoned railroad were removed. The New York State Department of Transportation used shredded tires as fill beneath the reconstructed roadway, and turned a large waste stockpile into part of the highway project. NYSDOT processed tires into large pieces known as tire shreds and used them as lightweight fill in selected embankment projects instead of sending the material to disposal sites. The state’s Tire Shred Initiative was developed alongside the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation as a way to address waste-tire stockpiles while using the material in highway construction.The I-87 project involved two bridges that carried the interstate over the abandoned Delaware and Hudson Railroad in Clinton County, south of Plattsburgh. Engineers removed them and filled the old railroad crossing with tire shreds and conventional earthen embankment material rather than rehabilitating or replacing the bridges. The new fill then supported the reconstructed roadway.The tyres became the fill beneath the roadNYSDOT’s own account says the tire-shred embankment represented approximately 1.1 million passenger tires and was completed in early 2005. The agency said the approach avoided the expense and labor that was associated with rehabilitating or replacing bridges that were no longer needed. A separate NYSDOT annual report states that work began in September 2004 under a $2.1 million contract, was completed in November 2005 and involved removing the northbound and southbound I-87 bridges over the abandoned railroad. The replacement used tire shreds together with earthen embankment fill.The tyres were shredded to specified sizes and placed in engineered sections. An earlier NYSDOT annual report described the project as a first-of-its-kind construction effort in the agency’s Region 7 and documented the installation of tire cells that contained hundreds of thousands of tires during the construction process. Tire shreds are much lighter than conventional soil and aggregate, which can reduce the load imposed on underlying ground, although the engineering design has to account for factors such as drainage, settlement and the potential for heat buildup in thick tire-shred fills.New York was also cleaning up tyre stockpilesNYSDOT records say that by November 2005, two projects under the Tire Shred Initiative had used the equivalent of about 1.4 million tires and helped remediate two waste-tire sites. The second project, on State Route 240X in Erie County, used nearly 300,000 tires in a new embankment section. A technical summary prepared for NYSDOT and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation describes the wider program and its environmental controls, and states that the I-87 Railroad Grade Crossing Elimination Project used approximately 1.1 million tires and was completed in spring 2005. The report also says tire-shred embankments were subject to design criteria that were intended to keep them above the water table and away from environmentally sensitive locations.The state monitored water quality around the projects, with testing for metals and other potential contaminants. The technical report said groundwater testing from the early projects showed very low levels of iron and manganese, while the design guidance took a conservative approach to site selection.NYSDOT had expanded tire-shred construction to several projects across the state by the late 2000s, and its program eventually used millions of passenger-tire equivalents and helped clean up large waste-tire sites. At the Plattsburgh crossing, however, the idea was that two obsolete bridges disappeared, the abandoned railroad corridor was filled, and roughly 1.1 million discarded tires became part of the engineered ground supporting I-87.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Commander who would not leave: The Phillora battle that won Lt Col Tarapore the Param Vir Chakra
articles.summary: News News: On this day in 1965, Lieutenant Colonel Ardeshir Burzorji Tarapore breathed his last on the battlefield, having led his regiment, the Poona Horse, thr.
articles.body: On this day in 1965, Lieutenant Colonel Ardeshir Burzorji Tarapore breathed his last on the battlefield, having led his regiment, the Poona Horse, through six days of relentless tank warfare against Pakistan in the Sialkot sector. Even after being wounded, he refused evacuation, staying with his men. By the time he fell, his regiment had destroyed roughly 60 enemy tanks while losing just nine of its own, one of the most lopsided armoured victories. For his leadership and courage, Lt Col Tarapore was posthumously awarded the Param Vir Chakra.Lieutenant Colonel Ardeshir Burzorji Tarapore, fondly remembered as Adi, was born in Bombay on August 18, 1923, into a family with a military lineage stretching back to an ancestor who served as a military leader under Shivaji. Commissioned into the 7th Hyderabad Infantry on January 1, 1942, Tarapore had set his heart on joining the armoured regiment of the Hyderabad State Forces, a dream that came true after Major General El-Edroos witnessed his bravery firsthand when he jumped into a bay to retrieve and safely dispose of a live grenade. He was subsequently transferred to the 1 Hyderabad Imperial Service Lancers, and after Hyderabad's merger with the Indian Union, his commission was revised to January 1, 1945, when he joined the storied Poona Horse.The 1965 war itself grew out of Pakistan's Operation Gibraltar, a mass infiltration attempt into Kashmir launched on August 5, followed by Operation Grand Slam on September 1, both of which were ultimately repelled by Indian forces, leading to full-scale war after Indian troops crossed the Radcliffe Line on September 6. Tasked with capturing the Sialkot sector, 1 Corps assigned Poona Horse, part of the 1st Armoured Division, the job of isolating Sialkot from Lahore by securing Phillora, Chawinda and the Tharoh Cross Roads.On September 11, as Tarapore's regiment moved to strike Phillora from the rear via Chawinda, it was suddenly counterattacked by heavy Pakistani armour advancing from Wazirwali. Tarapore held his ground, pressing the attack under continuous tank and artillery fire, and even after being wounded, refused evacuation. His regiment captured Wazirwali on September 14, then pushed on to Jassoran and Butur-Dograndi two days later, where his tank was hit repeatedly. Mortally wounded, Tarapore continued leading until his final moments. Under his command, the regiment destroyed roughly 60 Pakistani tanks against the loss of just nine of its own, a six-day feat of valour that earned Tarapore the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest wartime gallantry award, a legacy that endures as one of the defining chapters of India's military history.The Poona Horse itself carries a lineage dating back to 1817, raised under the Treaty of Poona negotiated by Mountstuart Elphinstone. Having fought in France, Palestine and Mesopotamia during the First World War, and as part of the British Eighth Army in the Second, the regiment went on to serve in Operation Polo in Hyderabad in 1948, before playing a decisive role in both the 1965 and 1971 wars, earning the Pakistani-coined title "Fakhr-e-Hind" for its battlefield conduct. The regiment has earned two Param Vir Chakras, the second won was awarded to Lt Arun Khetrapal in the 1971 war. Besides the two PVCs, members of the regiment have also earned four Victoria Crosses, the highest decoration for valour in the British empire.

articles.title: Oracle layoffs: Read the 6 am email Oracle Leadership reused for its second round of job cuts this year, telling employees 'today is your last working day'
articles.summary: Tech News News: Oracle's second mass layoff of 2026 came with a message its employees had already read once. The termination email that reached staff on Monday, signe.
articles.body: Oracle's second mass layoff of 2026 came with a message its employees had already read once. The termination email that reached staff on Monday, signed "Oracle Leadership", carried the same opening, the same reasoning and the same instructions as the note sent on March 31. Employees who had kept screenshots from the first round posted both versions side by side on Reddit, Blind and X. Apart from the date, they found nothing to tell them apart.The email runs to about 250 words and settles everything in its second paragraph. The role is gone, the decision followed "careful consideration" of business needs, and the working day on which it arrives is the last one. What follows is housekeeping: severance paperwork, a form to fill, a warning about company data. Oracle has not commented on the cuts, and the total number of employees affected is not yet known.Read the layoff email sent to Oracle employees on September 14, unchanged since March 31We are sharing some difficult news regarding your position.After careful consideration of Oracle's current business needs, we have made the decision to eliminate your role as part of a broader organizational change. As a result, today is your last working day.We are grateful for your dedication, hard work, and the impact you have made during your time with us.After signing your termination paperwork, you will be eligible to receive a severance package subject to the terms and conditions of the severance plan. You will receive an email from DocuSign to your Oracle email address with details on your severance and termination date.Immediate Action RequiredTo receive important follow-up information, including FAQs and separation documents to help you through this transition, you must provide a personal email address.Please click here to submit a personal email address immediately. If you make a submission error, please re-submit a new form. Please Note: The personal email address will only be used for correspondence regarding separation-related information and severance agreements.Access to your computer, email, voicemail, and files will be deactivated soon, and you will be unable to log into your computer. As a reminder, you are prohibited from downloading, copying or retaining (including emailing yourself any Oracle confidential information.Thank you for your contributions to our organization. If you have additional questions, please reach out to the HR team via the Ask HR page.Oracle Leadership.What Oracle's layoff email tells employees, and what it leaves outThe note gives no reason beyond a "broader organizational change". It names no team, no headcount and no manager to call. Severance is mentioned, but its terms are not. Those arrive later through DocuSign, and only after the employee signs termination paperwork.That order has drawn the most anger online. Employees on the r/employeesOfOracle forum said they were being asked to sign before they could see what they were signing for. One database engineer with four years at the company said the package came to seven weeks' pay, well short of what he had expected.Why the email asks for a personal address "immediately"Employees must submit a personal email address to receive FAQs and separation documents. The reason is spelled out a paragraph later: access to computers, email, voicemail and files "will be deactivated soon".For many, soon had already happened. Employees said logins stopped working around 4am Eastern on Monday and Slack went dark by 5.30am, so the 6am email landed in inboxes they could no longer open. Some were left waiting on a message to a personal address they had not had the chance to share. The same email also reminds recipients they cannot copy or forward any Oracle confidential information, which rules out emailing the note to themselves.Reports on social media named OCI, Fusion, NetSuite, Oracle Health, Customer Success Services and HR Technology among the affected groups. Several employees said they held "meets" or "exceeds expectations" ratings.Oracle layoffs in India hit mid- to senior-level staffThe cuts reached India the same day. Oracle began a fresh round in the country on Monday, hitting several mid- to senior-level employees in web development and maintenance, TOI reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Some sources put the number at 1,000 to 1,500 employees, a figure TOI could not independently verify. The count within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in India is also unconfirmed.In the March round, severance in India broadly followed the N+2 formula, where N is years of service paid in months. Unvested restricted stock was forfeited.That round also left unfinished business. More than 600 former employees signed a letter in April seeking better severance, extended healthcare and stock acceleration. Oracle said it would handle concerns one person at a time.Oracle's restructuring cost rises to $2.8 billionThe emails followed a regulatory filing on Friday in which Oracle raised its restructuring estimate by about $700 million. The fiscal 2026 plan is now expected to cost roughly $2.8 billion, and Oracle linked part of it to adopting AI across some functions.Spending on data centres keeps climbing. First-quarter capital expenditure hit $28.5 billion, up from $8.5 billion a year ago, and the full-year forecast holds at $90 billion to $95 billion. Oracle had already shed 21,000 jobs in the year to May 31, leaving about 141,000 employees before this week.The March email and Monday's email have the same wording, sender and send time.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: After SC rap, J&K govt finally clears Bilquis Mir for Asian Games after nearly a year
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: It has been a long court battle for international canoeing coach and umpire Bilquis Mir to obtain a no-objection certificate from the Jammu .
articles.body: SRINAGAR: It has been a long court battle for international canoeing coach and umpire Bilquis Mir to obtain a no-objection certificate from the Jammu and Kashmir government to join India’s kayaking and canoeing team for the 2026 Asian Games in Japan.“I really don’t know what I have done to deserve this treatment that for such a prestigious assignment Indian Kayaking and Canoeing Association had approached the high court and even the Supreme Court,” Mir said.“Bilquis Mir, Physical Education Teacher, is hereby accorded the requisite limited No Objection Certificate (NOC)/permission and is relieved for the purpose of joining and discharging the remaining assignment as Coach/Chief Coach of the Indian National Kayaking and Canoeing Team and for accompanying and assisting the Indian National Team in connection with the Asian Games, 2026,” read the order issued by the Department of Youth Services and Sports.Last week, the Supreme Court directed the Jammu and Kashmir government to issue a relieving order and no-objection certificate to Mir by September 15, allowing her to join the Indian national kayaking and canoeing team for the 2026 Asian Games.In its September 10 order in Indian Kayaking and Canoeing Association versus Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, a division bench of Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice Vipul M Pancholi observed, “in the present case, the Asian Games assignment is imminent. A remand to the competent authority for a fresh consideration, though ordinarily appropriate where an administrative decision is found defective, would in the peculiar circumstances amount to denial of effective relief, however, we cannot lose sight of the fact that the dispute has remained pending from February 2026 and that one international assignment has already been lost during the pendency of the proceedings.”The Indian Kayaking and Canoeing Association was not seeking Mir’s services for an indefinite private engagement. “The request emanated from a recognised National Sports Federation and concerned preparation of an Indian National Team for an identified international sporting event. The request was therefore required to be considered in that factual setting. At this juncture, it is apt and appropriate to refer the relevant dates which hold significance. The first request was made Feb 3, 2026. It was followed by reminders on Feb 1 , and April 2 2026. Yet no decision was taken before the appellant was compelled to invoke the writ jurisdiction on April 30 2026. Indeed, the High Court itself ultimately found that the delay was substantial and that such delay was capable of prejudicing the larger national interest,” the SC observed.This year, the kayaking association first sought Mir’s services on February 3, followed by reminders on March 1 and April 2. However, no decision was taken by the government, forcing the association to approach the High Court on April 30. The association cited the need for an experienced coach to prepare the Indian team for the Asian Games and sought her services from February 15 to September 2026.As no decision came from the government, the association sent reminders on March 1 and April 2, stressing the urgency of the coaching camp and the impact of Mir’s continued non-availability on the team’s preparation.The association then filed a case in the High Court on April 30, seeking directions to the authorities to grant the requisite permission and relieve Mir so that she could discharge her duties as coach of the Indian national team and participate in the Asian Games preparatory programme and related international assignments.On May 6, the High Court’s single bench directed the government to grant provisional permission to Mir to discharge her duties as chief coach/coach of the Indian national kayaking and canoeing team for the Asian Games and to travel to Hungary to officiate at the ICF Canoe Sprint World Cup.However, the Jammu and Kashmir government issued an order on June 19 denying her permission and a no-objection certificate for travel to Hungary and Japan. The government cited, among other grounds, an ongoing inquiry and issues concerning Mir’s B.P.Ed. qualification. It also said that the requisite documents had not been furnished through the prescribed mode and that vigilance clearance could not be processed.On July 28, the High Court’s single bench observed that the World Cup event had already passed and expressed concern that the June 19 government order had dealt with the matter substantially as an ordinary service issue without addressing the national sporting assignment for which the association had sought Mir’s services. The court said time was of the essence in deciding the writ petition.The Union Territory had filed an LPA against the interim order dated May 6. The matter was subsequently heard by the Supreme Court’s division bench. The bench said the Asian Games assignment was imminent and that a remand for fresh consideration would, in the circumstances, deny effective relief.The court quashed the June 19 government order as it denied Mir permission.Mir is a government employee serving as a physical education teacher in the Department of Youth Services and Sports, Jammu and Kashmir. The association had selected her as a coach for the Indian national kayaking and canoeing team’s preparation for the Asian Games. She was also selected to officiate as chief finish-line judge at the 2026 ICF Canoe Sprint World Cup in Szeged, Hungary, from May 8-10.Stay updated with the latest Srinagar news. articles.title: Gary Anderson: Top judge explains decision to free murderer from prison
articles.summary: Gary Anderson, who is serving 15 years for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018, remains on the run on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland's top judge has explained a court's decision to grant convicted killer Gary Anderson temporary release to attend his father's funeral, despite opposition from prison authorities.

Anderson, 29, who is one of two brothers jailed for life in 2023 for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry in 2018 , failed to return to Maghaberry prison on Monday.

The prison service had refused to grant Anderson compassionate temporary release (CTR) to attend the funeral, but that was overturned by a court on Sunday.

The Office of the Lady Chief Justice (LCJ) said the court had held that the governor's decision not to grant CTR was "not substantiated by the evidence provided to the court".

The Northern Ireland Courts Service (NICS) confirmed that the judge who took the decision was Mr Justice Rooney.

"This was an individual judicial decision, and it is not appropriate for this office to make any further comment," the Office of LCJ said.

Anderson's brother Sean, who is serving 17 years for the murder of Karol Kelly, also challenged the decision not to release him from Magilligan Prison to attend the funeral, but that was upheld.

"The application was brought on the grounds that the decisions breached the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) rights of the applicants," the Office of the LCJ said.

"The court found that the decision by the governor in respect of Sean Anderson was carried out lawfully and refused the application for leave to challenge the decision."

Anderson was released from Maghaberry Prison on Monday to attend his father's funeral, but absconded from his court-approved chaperone.

It is unclear who that chaperone is or what powers, if any, were given to that person.

The funeral took place at St Mary's Church in the Creggan area of Derry on Monday morning followed by cremation in Letterkenny, County Donegal, that afternoon.

Anderson was not granted permission to cross the border to attend the cremation.

The conditions of his release, as follows, have been confirmed to BBC News NI:

The applicant will be released from Maghaberry prison and brought to Derry courthouse by 09:30 BST to return at 11:30 BST

The applicant is to be collected by (named person) by car and remain with him throughout

He is to attend only the funeral of his father at St Mary's Church and must stay within confines of the church

Applicant's representatives must contact the Judicial Review Office to advice all went to plan

The applicant is not to consume alcohol or any non-prescribed medication

The applicant is not to use any electronic communication device

The applicant is to return to prison directly from the Derry courthouse

Speaking on Wednesday, Justice Minister Naomi Long said she believed the prison service had reached "the right conclusion" in relation to Anderson's release.

"They have the experience of doing these assessments on an ongoing basis. They felt it wasn't safe on this occasion for him to be released," Long said.

"But he has rights. He was able to exercise those rights in the court and a judge with that information reached a different conclusion."

That, the minster said, is "part of the process" and "entirely legitimate".

Long said the majority of prisoners on short term release return to custody as required.

"This is an unusual situation that we find ourselves in but it is a deeply concerning one," she said.

"It is not about apportioning blame, it is about trying to find out how we ensure this doesn't happen again but also how we get this person back into custody."

The minister, who urged Anderson to hand himself over to police, said he is "a threat to the public and he is potentially also at risk."

However, the DUP MLA Trevor Clarke, who sits on the policing board, said the whole process needed looked at.

"I think there's clear evidence that there was an issue in this case and that's now been borne out because this person hasn't come back," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"All of the things that the courts have involved themselves in this one, I think, has been wrong.

"A chaperone as opposed to a proper prison guard, this is an individual who cannot even handcuff the person while they're chaperoned, so all of the safeguards that could have been put in place weren't put in place."

On Wednesday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed that Anderson was last seen in the Eastway area of Creggan in Derry.

They also confirmed that they were liaising with An Garda Síochána (Irish police).

articles.title: In 2018, Thailand placed a 1,800kg statue underwater to support coral restoration, with more than 5,000 coral fragments transplanted onto an artificial reef
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore how Thailand's remarkable 1,800kg Mazu statue is contributing to coral reef restoration, creating a new marine habitat with over 5,000 coral transplants.
articles.body: In 2018, on the seabed off Koh Tao, a Thai island in the Gulf of Thailand, an unusual structure appeared. It was a sculpture of Mazu, weighing 1,800 kilograms, a Chinese sea goddess associated with protection at sea. The statue was installed as the centrepiece of an artificial reef. About 36 smaller pyramid-shaped structures were placed underwater, along the sculpture, carrying thousands of coral transplants. The aim was to provide additional hard surfaces for coral growth and create a habitat that marine organisms could use. The World Economic Forum reported in June 2020 that Global Coralition, working with conservation group Eco Koh Tao, had built the sculpture in 2018. The organisation’s page also says that Mazu was deployed in 2018.An underwater statue was transformed into the centre of an artificial reefAn unusual combination of art and marine conservation was brought together by the project. Global Coralition worked with Eco Koh Tao to install the sculpture and its surrounding structures, with the aim of attracting attention to coral restoration while giving transplanted corals suitable habitats to grow. Mazu has been described by the organisation as a symbol of marine protection. The organisation also says that the installation has subsequently turned into a focus for conservation activity around Koh Tao.The project opted to use a recognisable cultural figure as its centrepiece rather than creating an artificial reef entirely from anonymous blocks. The World Economic Forum describes the use of art to get the local communities, divers and other interested parties to participate in marine conservation through the Global Coralition project. The presence of pyramids increased the number of man-made surfaces for the transplantation of coral. More than 5,000 coral fragments were transplanted onto the pyramids. This gave the young, translocated coral colonies a stable surface to settle instead of depending solely on natural hard surfaces.The marine species quickly colonised the structure. Mazu became covered with crustose coralline algae within four months after the placement of the structure in the ocean. The crustose coralline algae are calcifying algae found in coral reef ecosystems.Research at Koh Tao argues that artificial reefs are not natural reefsPublished in Marine Environmental Research in 2021, a peer-reviewed study provides context for projects like Mazu. The paper examined coral recruitment at artificial substructures around Koh Tao and compared the resulting coral communities with those at nearby natural reefs. It included 2,677 coral recruits from nine sites.The findings of the research suggested that artificial reefs can support distinct ecological and functional roles. The data also showed that depth was one factor associated with differences in coral community structures, while the diversity of recruits could not simply be explained by coral spawning dynamics.The study is especially relevant because artificial structures are widely used in Thailand. The researchers of the study noted that concrete structures and decommissioned vessels had been deployed in Thai waters as artificial substrates for coral restoration and marine recreation. In conclusion, the writers of the article pointed out that these artificial reefs have to be seen as playing certain ecological roles and not being used as a replacement for natural reefs. In this case, the Mazu Project can be best described as an artificial-reef and coral-transplantation project rather than a replication of the natural reef.Notably, Mazu offered visibility, an advantage that a conventional concrete reef might not have. The installation attracts hundreds of divers every week and has become a crucial point for marine conservation awareness. Mazu has become an example of how art can be combined with coral-restoration work. The unusual centrepiece also helped turn an ecological intervention into something divers could recognise and visit. Rather than a restoration site that remained largely invisible to the public, the project gave the conservation effort a physical landmark beneath the water.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Guernsey and Jersey secure new electricity import deal with EDF
articles.summary: The deal with the French company is set to run for another four years from 2028.
articles.body:
Electricity companies in Guernsey and Jersey have signed a new four-year contract with EDF energy to continue importing electricity from Europe from 2028.

The agreement will take effect on 1 January 2028, when the islands' current agreement with the French energy company comes to an end.

Currently most of electricity needed for the islands is met through imported power supplied via subsea cables linking them to the European grid through the Channel Islands Electricity Grid network.

Guernsey Electricity chief executive Alan Bates said the deal would help secure the islands' energy supply while supporting efforts to cut carbon emissions.

The agreement continues the long-standing relationship between Guernsey Electricity, Jersey Electricity and EDF.

Jersey's first undersea cable was installed in 1985 and the Jersey-Guernsey cable entered service in 2000.

Bates said he was delighted with the deal to continue importing low carbon electricity, which would reduce the need to use the fossil fuel powered generators at the Vale Power Station.

"We can also import low carbon electricity at a price generally lower than that of generating on island, which helps to manage the impact of electricity prices on islanders," he said.

He said the contract would also allow the company to continue using forward purchasing arrangements to help protect customers from volatility in wholesale energy markets and reduce the impact of price fluctuations on local electricity tariffs.

Jersey Electricity chief executive Chris Ambler said the agreement was important for the future of the island with more households moving away from fossil fuel heating and the number of electric vehicles continuing to grow.

"Electricity is becoming increasingly important to the island's economy and everyday life," he said.

"This agreement gives us greater visibility over our future supply arrangements while allowing us to continue investing in the resilience of Jersey's electricity network."

articles.title: 'Have a spine, don't lie down in front of Trump': Rahul flays PM Modi over 'UPI tax'
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday attacked Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the Centre’s new Merchant Discou.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday attacked Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the Centre’s new Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework for Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions, accusing the government of yielding to pressure from the United States and urging Modi to “have a spine”.In a video posted on X, Rahul referred to former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi while drawing a comparison with PM Modi over the new UPI measures.“Indiraji was once asked whether she leans left or right, and her response was, ‘I don't lean left or right. I stand straight’,” Gandhi said. He then turned to the UPI framework, alleging that Modi had adopted a different approach.“Modiji has a completely diff concept, he's neither left or right he has decided to completely lie down straight and in front of Donald Trump. He's put a tax on every single Indian person by taxing UPI and giving huge amount op money to the United States,” the former Congress president added.He said, “Modiji, please stop lying down in front of the US. Have a spine, stand up and withdraw the UPI tax. Thank you."The Congress has described the new MDR as a “Modi tax” and alleged that the decision was linked to pressure from the US. The party has also criticised the government’s handling of the policy, calling it another example of what general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh termed a “FAST (First Announce, Subsequently Think) move”.Ramesh earlier questioned the timing of the decision, saying, “Decision Making in Modi Govt -- Aug 6: Hon'ble Finance Minister says 'no decision has been taken on MDR'. Aug 10: FM in Parliament says 'No MDR framework has yet been finalised'. Sep 14: Notification is issued. Within 24 hrs, MDR charges introduced.”Earlier in the day, the finance ministry rejected allegations of foreign pressure behind the revised UPI framework, clarifying that changes in regulations stem entirely from domestic priorities. It said UPI said MDR would apply only to specified merchant transactions above Rs 2,000, while person-to-person UPI payments would remain free. Around 96 per cent of person-to-merchant transactions will remain unaffected.Under the framework, a 0.4 per cent MDR will apply to specified merchant payments above Rs 2,000 from October 15, capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. The charge is payable within the merchant-payment ecosystem, not by consumers.A flat Rs 5 charge will apply to utility bill payments, fuel purchases, insurance premiums, railway tickets and several government services.The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has said the revenue will support infrastructure resilience, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, innovation and customer service. UPI processed 24,508.96 million transactions worth nearly Rs 29.82 lakh crore in August 2026, according to NPCI data.The new framework is set to take effect from October 15, putting the focus on how merchants, banks and payment platforms absorb the revised costs and whether the change affects pricing or the wider adoption of digital payments.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2013, an archivist traced BBC overseas shipment records to a Nigerian television relay station; he found 11 Doctor Who film recordings, including nine episodes still missing in Britain
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a remarkable discovery, an archivist in Nigeria uncovered 11 film cans of Doctor Who episodes, including nine that had been missing from the UK archives for decades. This major find drops the total number of missing Doctor Who episodes to 97 and highlights the ongoing search for lost television treasures.
articles.body: For most of its existence, people considered television disposable. Film reels were junked to free up storage space, broadcasters recorded over old cassettes to save money, and no one at the BBC in the 1960s could have predicted that the broadcasts they were casually erasing would eventually be regarded as cultural treasures. Because of this shortsighted tendency, a large portion of early British television has simply vanished, and its eventual resuscitation usually makes news decades later. This technique particularly affected Doctor Who. Of the 253 episodes of Doctor Who produced between 1963 and 1969, more than 100 were missing from the BBC archives by the time the worldwide search for surviving copies began.Following the paper trail to NigeriaThe specialist was Philip Morris, the proprietor of a company that specialises in tracking down missing television material of this sort. Morris’s company, Television International Enterprises Archive, says his method relies heavily on tracing historical shipment records because old programmes were often sent to overseas broadcasters and later left in storage after their original transmissions.The paper trail took Morris to a television relay station in Jos, a city in central Nigeria, where he was working with the Nigerian Television Authority on an unrelated archival assignment. He spotted several film cans sitting in a dusty storeroom, still marked with their original masking tape labels. When he saw the words ‘Doctor Who’ on the cans and checked the story codes, he realised he had found something importantNine episodes unseen in Britain for decadesIn total, 11 canisters were recovered from the Nigerian relay station, containing full adventures with Patrick Troughton as the Second Doctor, first broadcast from December 1967 to March 1968. Two of the reels turned out to be copies of episodes previously possessed by the BBC, but nine were actually missing, not seen anywhere in Britain since their first transmission nearly half a century ago. Five came from a story entitled The Enemy of the World, which concluded the six-part adventure that was paired with an episode already in the archive. Four came from The Web of Fear, the evocative tale in which the Doctor battled robotic Yeti beneath the streets of London.The find was exceptional by any metric. Morris said on the BBC's own Doctor Who website that the discovery was "possibly the largest haul of lost episodes recovered in twenty-five or thirty years." The haul instantly dropped the total number of missing episodes from 106 down to 97. The recovered material was presented at a London screening attended by Frazer Hines and Deborah Watling, who had played companions Jamie and Victoria, along with writer Mark Gatiss, who described the discovery as ‘thrilling’ and ‘almost impossible to believe.A single canister that got awayNot all of the recovered material made it safely back to Britain. Episode three of The Web of Fear, which contains the first appearance of the character later known as the Brigadier, disappeared before it could be returned to the BBC. Contemporary accounts said it was believed to have been taken and possibly sold to a private collector. The episode therefore remained the one missing piece of an otherwise complete six-part story.The British Film Institute, which holds an annual event for the screening of newly rediscovered British television material, has continued to showcase fresh finds from private collectors and overseas archives since then, proof that the Nigerian relay station was not necessarily the last hiding place of its kind. Since Doctor Who is built around time travel, it is fitting that some of its earliest adventures spent decades undiscovered before finally returning home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: The United States has advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia amid renewed security threats from Iranian missile and drone attacks, .
articles.body: The United States has advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia amid renewed security threats from Iranian missile and drone attacks, armed conflict and terrorism. It also issued a separate Level 4 "Do Not Travel" warning for the Yemen border.“Reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia due to risk of Iranian drone and missile targeting of American interests, armed conflict, terrorism, exit bans”, the US Embassy in Riyadh said in the advisory.The US State Department's Level 3 advisory, issued on September 15, comes as Saudi Arabia faces a fresh wave of attacks linked to Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including the interception of a drone south of the holy city of Mecca.It said some parts of the country face higher risks and warned that commercial flights, while still operating, have faced significant disruptions.Why has the US issued a travel warning for Saudi Arabia?The advisory comes amid a wider escalation in the region. The State Department said that since hostilities between the US and Iran began on February 28, there has been an ongoing threat of drone and missile attacks from Iran.It said missiles and drones have been launched towards Saudi Arabia, while Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen have also threatened further attacks on the kingdom.Saudi Arabia has faced a series of recent Houthi attacks, including strikes targeting Saudi territory and military infrastructure. On Tuesday, Saudi air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered the holy city's restricted airspace, according to the Saudi-led coalition. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki described Mecca's security as a "red line".Saudi Arabia had also issued security alerts in Mecca, Jeddah and other areas following recent Houthi attacks. The alerts were later lifted after authorities said the immediate threat had passed.Yemen border under ‘Do Not Travel’ warningThe US has placed the Saudi-Yemen border region under a separate Level 4 "Do Not Travel" warning because of the threat of terrorism. The State Department said armed groups in Yemen have attacked Saudi border towns and other locations with drones, missiles and rockets, putting people near the border at increased risk.US government employees working in Saudi Arabia are restricted from travelling within 20 miles of the Yemen border. They also face restrictions on travel to Qatif, Jizan, Asir and Najran, with special authorisation required for travel to several of these areas.The advisory also warned Americans about possible terrorist attacks at airports, military facilities, energy sites, hotels, transport hubs, tourist locations and crowded areas.It cautioned that Saudi authorities can detain people over social media posts considered critical, offensive or disruptive to public order. articles.title: US House votes 220-204 to curb Trump’s Iran war powers; 7 Republicans back move
articles.summary: US News: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday voted 220-204 to require President Donald Trump to end US military involvement in hostilities with Iran wit.
articles.body: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday voted 220-204 to require President Donald Trump to end US military involvement in hostilities with Iran without congressional authorisation, marking the third time lawmakers have passed a war powers resolution seeking to limit his authority over the conflict. Seven Republicans joined all voting Democrats in backing the measure.The vote came as the Iran war entered its seventh month and on the same day the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that US military operations against Iran had cost the Pentagon about $38 billion through August 1. The CBO said continued fighting could cost another $2 billion to $3 billion a month, depending on the intensity of operations.The resolution, led by Democratic Representative Seth Moulton of Massachusetts, directs the administration to remove US armed forces from hostilities against Iran, while allowing US personnel to remain where necessary to defend American or allied forces and bases in the region. The White House has argued that such resolutions are not legally binding.Seven Republicans back the measureSeven Republicans voted with Democrats, up from four Republicans who supported the two previous House resolutions. The three Republicans backing the latest measure for the first time were Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn of Iowa and Nancy Mace of South Carolina, according to CNN.The four Republicans who had previously supported the war powers resolutions were Thomas Massie of Kentucky, Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.House Republican leaders have not formally required members to vote one way or another on the resolutions. Trump, however, has publicly criticised Republicans who have opposed his Iran policy, making the votes an increasingly visible test of Republican support for his handling of the war, CNN reported.Why the House voted againThe latest vote is part of a months-long effort by House Democrats to force lawmakers to take formal positions on the continuing military operation.The House first approved a similar war powers resolution in June and followed it with another in July. Neither reached Trump's desk. The latest measure therefore represents the third House attempt to restrict the president's authority over the Iran conflict.The timing is also significant. The House is nearing its final voting sessions before lawmakers return to their districts to campaign ahead of the November midterm elections. Democrats have sought to put Republicans on record over the war as voters confront its economic and military consequences.Senate hurdle remainsThe resolution still needs to clear the Senate before it could reach the White House.The Senate previously passed a similar war powers resolution after securing enough Republican support. But that effort collapsed after a Republican senator changed his vote following pressure from the Trump administration, according to CNN and AP. Democrats are expected to try again later this week, but it remains uncertain whether they can secure enough Senate votes.Even if Congress ultimately approves the measure, the Trump administration has opposed the effort and has previously maintained that Congress cannot use the War Powers Resolution to direct the president in this manner. Previous House resolutions never reached Trump's desk.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: White-tailed eagle chicks fledge again amid reintroduction project
articles.summary: The Forestry England and the Roy Dennis Wildlife Foundation reintroduction project began in 2019.
articles.body:
White-tailed eagle chicks have successfully fledged from wild nests in England for the fourth consecutive year.

Two out of five pairs of eagles released by a reintroduction project successfully bred and raised young with one chick fledging from a nest in Dorset and two more in Sussex.

The project, run by Forestry England and the Roy Dennis Wildlife Foundation, aims to return the species to England . Nine birds have been born in the wild since it began in 2019.

"This year's breeding success is another important milestone in the return of this lost species to England; it shows what can be achieved by very skilled wildlife managers," Roy Dennis OBE from the foundation said.

The foundation has called the breeding attempts "remarkable", adding that one of the male adult birds has only one leg after losing it five years ago.

Human persecution had caused the bird's extinction, with the last pair breeding in southern England in 1780.

"Restoring a species takes many years and requires the support of a wide range of communities and organisations, in particular landowners and farmers," Dennis added.

Steve Egerton-Read, white-tailed eagle project officer for Forestry England, said: "We are delighted that these three chicks made it through and will be closely watching their progress as they begin to explore the landscape."

To date, 56 young white-tailed eagles have been released including, for the first time this year, additional releases of six birds at Exmoor National Park, in partnership with Exmoor National Park Authority.

articles.title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental defenders, report says
articles.summary: The two countries accounted for 52% of killings of environmental activists in 2025, according to Global Witness.
articles.body:
Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness .

Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26.

Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012.

Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states.

Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years.

Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says.

Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed.

Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining.

Last week, Jacob Guachetá Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed.

While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory.

Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024.

As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found.

Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders.

The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported.

articles.title: Husband who drugged and raped wife for 20 years no longer part of trial
articles.summary: Twelve other men are still due to stand trial accused of serious sexual offences against the same woman.
articles.body:
A man who drugged and raped his wife for more than 20 years without her knowledge will no longer be involved in a trial involving other defendants, a jury has heard.

The husband, aged in his 60s and from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, has admitted a total of 60 offences against the woman including rape, assault by penetration, administering a substance with intent and sharing indecent images without her consent.

Twelve other men are still due to go on trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court accused of serious sexual offences - including rape - against the same woman.

The nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, have been asked to return to court on 5 October.

The court has heard the husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, has admitted abusing his wife since 2004.

He had already pleaded guilty to 15 offences against her going back to 2022, but admitted to a further 45 counts on Monday.

His wife, who was comforted by other members of her family, watched from the public gallery as he answered "guilty" to dozens of charges.

The other defendants in the case are alleged to have sexually abused her since September 2018.

A 14th man has also pleaded guilty to sexual offences against the woman.

On Wednesday morning the court heard that when the jurors were sworn in on 4 September they were given a questionnaire which included a short summary of the prosecution case.

Trial judge Maurice Greene told them: "You were told, amongst other things, that the prosecution case concerns allegations of sexual offences by a number of men on a female.

"You were told 14 men had been identified and one was [her husband].

"No doubt you will be wondering why you have not been back since.

"Some of you may have seen or heard on the news on Monday that a man from Stockport had pleaded guilty to drugging and raping his wife, and had admitted multiple offences including rape, attempted rape, sexual assault and administering a substance with intent.

"Now his identity is prohibited in the public domain to protect [his wife's] identity. Logical and obvious you may think.

"Of course the man who pleaded guilty was [the husband], so he will no longer be a defendant in this case. As a result of these pleas there is work to be done by parties in this case."

Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire

Daniel Rayner, 42, from, Whitstable, Kent

David Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, Derbyshire

Judge Greene told the jury he expected the prosecution to open the case on 5 October and that the trial should be completed by 18 December.

articles.body: PATNA: In a shocking display of anger over an inter-caste marriage, a family in Purnia allegedly performed the symbolic funeral of their 18-year-old daughter after she eloped with her boyfriend and married him in court.The family prepared an effigy carrying her photograph, took out a funeral procession through the locality and performed symbolic last rites after the woman admitted in a local court that she had married the man of her choice.The incident took place at Chapay village in the Town police station area of Purnia on Tuesday.Riya, a Part-I college student allegedly eloped with 24-year-old Minal Kumar on September 8 and married him in a court.Her father, Manoj Kumar Goswami, had subsequently approached Maranga police and filed a missing complaint, fearing that his daughter had been abducted.According to villagers, Riya and Minal had been in a relationship for around three years. Their houses are reportedly only about 100metres apart.The two initially saw each other while Riya travelled to college and gradually began meeting and talking.Two days ago, police reportedly recovered Riya from Delhi and produced her before court, where her statement was recorded.When she reportedly spoke in favour of Minal and said she had married him voluntarily, her father was deeply upset. He then decided to symbolically end his relationship with his daughter through a funeral ceremony.By Monday night, preparations for the unusual ceremony had begun.According to the villagers, the family made an effigy of Riya and prepared a poster carrying her photograph. Villagers were invited the next morning to participate in the procession.The effigy was then carried out from the house on a bier in a funeral procession through the village. People reportedly raised the Hindu funeral chant “Ram Naam Satya Hai”, before Manoj performed the symbolic cremation.The family also said it intends to perform rituals associated with death, including shraddha and pind-daan between the 10th and 13th days.Manoj said the family had already arranged Riya’s marriage with a man from Bhagalpur who works as a government teacher. According to him, the match had been finalised for Rs 6 lakh and the wedding was scheduled for November.“We had started preparing for the marriage. In the meantime, my daughter ran away and married of her own choice. Now what will I tell the other family?
