articles.title: DoJ accuses Russia of trying to kill Ukraine allies in US and Europe
articles.summary: The FBI says five men "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".
articles.body:
The US Department of Justice (DoJ) has accused Russia of plotting to murder Ukrainian allies in the US and Europe.

In a statement on Tuesday, the DoJ charged five men allegedly connected to the Russian Intelligence Services (RIS). The men are accused of paying, or trying to pay, people in the US and overseas to target those "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine".

"It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil," Attorney General Todd Blanche. All those accused remain at large.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday Moscow will not comment until it hears or sees "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

It is not clear if the five accused are in the United States, or in a different location.

Washington has charged all five men with participating in a conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum 20-year prison sentence.

Three of the defendants are "high-ranking members of the RIS network", the DoJ said.

Among them are Russian father and son Yuri Khrameev, 63, and Kirill Khrameev, 27. Khrameev senior was a colonel in the Russian intelligence services and his son is an officer in the Federal Security Service of Russia (FSB).

The third high-ranking suspect is Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a 35-year-old Cuban national who the US describe as "an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia who has coordinated attacks for the RIS network".

Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, are the other two defendants.

The pair are accused of recruiting or attempting to recruit US-based individuals to "surveil and attempt to murder a prominent US-based Russian dissident".

The FBI's James Barnacle said the group "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on US soil and around the world".

One of the incidents is as recent as this summer. The DoJ described how the RIS network was able to recruit someone in the US to surveil and eventually murder a Russian dissident in the US.

Suarez allegedly sent the recruit to two locations linked to the victim with "explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance". In exchange, the recruit was offered between $1,000 (£743) and $1,500.

Suarez and Castro are said to have offered an additional $40,000 if the US resident could "eliminate" the dissident.

The DoJ said the RIS recruit did not go through with it, which led Suarez to try and recruit "multiple other individuals within the United States". He allegedly offered "substantial sums of money to carry out the targeting of US based victims".

The release by the DoJ goes on to list other instances in which the accused allegedly tried to recruit others to kill those who were a perceived threat to Russia.

It said that in 2025, Khrameev junior allegedly recruited a US citizen to surveil and murder someone in Lithuania who was "telling lies about Russia". The release quotes Khrameev as saying the purpose was to target "all the countries that are helping Ukraine".

His father, Khrameev senior, is said to have offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the individual in Lithuania for "spreading dirt about my country" and "distorting history".

Khrameev senior, Suarez and Castro are the only ones also charged with "participating in a conspiracy to commit murder for hire". If found guilty, this charge carries a maximum 10-year prison sentence.

It is not the first time authorities thwart threats of this kind.

Last month, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained an individual allegedly working for the Kremlin and who was plotting to murder an American-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw.

Tusk told reporters the American-Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime", adding: "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons."

In 2024, German authorities were reportedly warned by US intelligence of a Russian plot to kill Armin Papperger, the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall.

Moscow dismissed the accusation at the time, with Kremlin spokesman Peskov saying: "It's all presented in the style of another fake story, so such reports cannot be taken seriously."

The fresh accusations from the DoJ come at a time of closer relations between Moscow and Washington following US President Donald Trump's return to the White House in 2025.

A few weeks ago, the head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) visited Moscow for talks with figures from Russia's intelligence services - an unconventional move that led to speculation.

The Kremlin confirmed that talks between John Ratcliffe and the intelligence services had taken place. President Trump did not say what was discussed but described the meeting as "semi-routine".

articles.title: In 2012, an Idaho man built one bed in his garage for a child sleeping on the floor; 14 years later, the idea has delivered nearly 396,000 beds through 400+ chapters
articles.summary: US News: A single homemade bunk bed built in an Idaho garage in 2012 has grown into a large volunteer movement focused on one simple goal: making sure children.
articles.body: A single homemade bunk bed built in an Idaho garage in 2012 has grown into a large volunteer movement focused on one simple goal: making sure children have a proper place to sleep. According to Sleep in Heavenly Peace (SHP), the organisation that grew from founder Luke Mickelson’s first bed-building effort, what began as a small Christmas project has expanded to more than 400 chapters across the United States and Canada. Over the years, volunteers have built and delivered hundreds of thousands of beds to children in need, turning a personal act of service into a wider effort to address what the organisation calls child bedlessness.How one garage project beganThe story started in December 2012, when Mickelson decided to spend part of Christmas building bunk beds for children who did not have beds of their own. The first project took place in his garage in Twin Falls, Idaho. Mickelson and people close to him built beds and prepared to deliver them to local children. One of the people who joined that first effort was Jordan Allen, Mickelson's childhood friend. Allen later recalled that the group initially saw the activity largely as a woodworking project. That changed when they delivered one of the beds to a young child who had been sleeping on the floor.The experience showed them that a basic piece of furniture could have a much larger meaning for a child and family facing difficult circumstances. The first beds were simple, handmade bunk beds. But the idea behind them was straightforward: children should not have to sleep on floors because their families cannot afford a bed.From a few volunteers to an organisationThe initial projects continued beyond that first Christmas. Mickelson and Allen kept building beds, with volunteers joining them and helping with deliveries. By the end of 2013, the effort had developed enough momentum for Mickelson and others to formally establish Sleep in Heavenly Peace as a nonprofit organisation.Its central message became “No Kid Sleeps on the Floor in Our Town.” The model was designed around local participation. Rather than relying only on a central organisation to build and distribute every bed, SHP developed chapters that could organise volunteers, collect materials, build beds and identify families who needed them. That chapter-based approach allowed the original Idaho project to be replicated in other communities.How the bed-building model worksThe organisation's work involves more than assembling wooden frames. Volunteers help build beds, prepare mattresses and bedding, and participate in deliveries to families. Local chapters also work with community groups, businesses and donors to obtain the materials and funding required for the programme. The result is a process in which people can contribute at different stages, from helping construct a bed to providing bedding or assisting with delivery.SHP's growth demonstrates how the chapter model has allowed the project to spread well beyond its original community. The organisation now has more than 400 chapters across the United States and Canada, according to its website.Bunks Across America brings chapters togetherOne of the organisation's largest annual initiatives is Bunks Across America, which brings SHP chapters together for concentrated bed-building and delivery efforts. The 2026 event ran from September 5 to 12, with SHP aiming to involve 15,000 volunteers across 250 chapters and build more than 12,000 beds during the week.The event has grown considerably over the years. In 2025, the seventh annual Bunks Across America involved 209 chapters and nearly 13,000 volunteers, who helped build more than 10,000 beds. SHP said that by then, more than 300,000 children had received beds since the organisation was founded in 2012. The annual campaign gives volunteers a common period in which to work towards the same objective, while individual chapters continue their work throughout the year.Why a bed can mean more than furnitureThe organisation's original experience also shaped the way its volunteers view the programme. During one of the first deliveries, volunteers encountered a child whose sleeping arrangement was little more than a pile of clothes on the floor. When the newly built bunk bed was assembled, the child's reaction became a defining moment for those involved.For SHP, the purpose of the programme therefore extends beyond providing a physical object. A bed can give a child a dedicated sleeping space and provide a sense of comfort and security within the home. That idea has remained central to the organisation as it has expanded.An idea that kept growingThe contrast between SHP's beginnings and its current scale is considerable. What started with Mickelson building beds in his garage has developed into a network of hundreds of chapters and thousands of volunteers. The organisation's 2025 campaign alone recorded 10,075 beds built, 12,955 volunteers and 48,476 volunteer hours. The growth has also changed the nature of the original idea. It is no longer simply one person building a bed for one child; it is a community-based system that allows people across different cities and states to take part in the same mission. Fourteen years after the first garage build, the project continues to revolve around the same basic need that inspired it in 2012: ensuring that children have a bed of their own.What began with one Idaho garage and a handful of volunteers has since become a network spanning hundreds of communities, with nearly 396,000 beds delivered, according to the organisation's current figures. articles.title: Bonnie Greer: British-American author and critic dies at 77
articles.summary: Her husband says the playwright and cultural and political commentator died after a brief illness.
articles.body:
British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins described her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan.

She moved to the UK in 1986 and she became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a panellist on programmes like Newsnight Review and Question Time.

Once named by the Observer as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled topics around culture, race and public institutions.

Speaking to the Guardian in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: "When I wake up in the morning, I'm just myself. It's only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world."

She added: "I tell black women all the time, 'Don't apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard'."

Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London's Kingston University.

Her published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a critical biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes.

She was awarded the Verity Bargate Award for best play for Munda Negra, and also wrote the novels Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009).

Also in 2009, her memoir and music history, Obama Music, was published.

Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts.

In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

articles.title: Andy Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments
articles.summary: The prime minister insists he is prepared to take "difficult decisions" at next month's Budget.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has insisted he is prepared to take "difficult decisions" on the economy, after a former Bank of England chief economist said investors were worried about his willingness to cut spending.

Speaking on Tuesday, Andy Haldane, who has advised Burnham on the economy, claimed financial markets had grown wary of his economic plans and now considered his premiership a "traditional tax and spend socialist government".

But the PM rejected this, adding that he would not take risks with the economy and had already made difficult choices since taking office.

It comes as recent rises to the cost of UK borrowing worsened the political options facing the government ahead of next month's Budget.

Haldane said the prime minister's was facing a "straight choice" between raising taxes and cutting spending at the yearly spending statement due on 28 October.

In an interview with LBC, he urged him not to raise taxes further, but said investors were questioning whether he was prepared to risk anger from Labour backbenchers by making reductions in public expenditure.

"The fiscal Achilles Heel of this government thus far has been its unwillingness and/or inability to cut public spending," he told the radio station.

"Within financial markets, we've gone from the cautious optimism of the summer months to the studied scepticism of September. The market now suspects that this is a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos."

Petrol and diesel price rises push UK inflation higher

Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises

Speaking during a visit earlier on Wednesday, Burnham conceded that next month's Budget would be "challenging", blaming the "situation in the Middle East" for rising inflation in recent months .

But he rejected Haldane's characterisation of how markets viewed the government, telling broadcasters: "That doesn't tell the story. We are not that."

He added he had already taken difficult decisions on public spending, including "reprioritising" some government spending over the summer to pay for his early cost of living announcements , and scrapping the rollout of digital ID.

He added: "So it's not the case that we aren't going to take difficult decisions. We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track."

Burnham has recommitted to manifesto promises made by Labour at the last general election not to raise the main rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance, significantly curbing his options to raise revenue.

At the same time, he has also pledged to stick to the previous government's debt and spending targets, a task that will be made harder by recent increases to the cost of servicing the UK's existing pile of debt.

There have been predictions that the rise, combined with a worsening economic backdrop from the Iran war, are likely to significantly thin the £24bn buffer against those targets he inherited from the Starmer government.

Since coming to office, Burnham has committed around £1.8bn towards cost of living interventions, some of which is due to be funded by reallocating money within the existing budgets of government departments.

But a proposal to fund a VAT cut on household electricity bills using money earmarked for the digital ID programme drew criticism from a Starmer ally, who pointed out that funding for that scheme had itself not been confirmed .

The prime minister has also promised extra defence funding promised by Starmer before his exit over the summer, although a decision on when to hit a target to spend 3% of GDP on the military has been left to next year.

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis test Mecca’s sacred shield
articles.summary: WhatsApp groups and social media across Saudi Arabia lit up on Tuesday with variations of the same message: The Houthis are attacking Mecca.
articles.body:
WhatsApp groups and social media across Saudi Arabia lit up on Tuesday with variations of the same message: The Houthis are attacking Mecca. Photos of the Kaaba and prayers of "God protect this country" spread after Saudi civil defense issued an alert for Islam's holiest city, the first since the war began, before lifting it minutes later. Some questioned whether it was an error or a test, while others condemned their "fellow Muslims" for threatening what is holy.

Over the past six months, there was a sense that Mecca would provide a shield for western Saudi Arabia. As sirens went off over Riyadh and the Eastern Province, people in the Hejaz assumed no one would dare approach what all Muslims deem sacred. Tuesday's alert punctured that logic. While nothing was hit — Saudi authorities said a drone was intercepted — the taboo has been broken. Nothing is holy in war.

articles.title: India vs Afghanistan 3rd T20I 2026 predicted lineups, will Vaibhav Sooryavanshi return to starting XI for dead rubber clash in Delhi?
articles.summary: With India already taking the three-match series last night, the third match is all set to be dead rubber but can Vaibhav Sooryavanshi return to open?
articles.body:
India face Afghanistan in a dead rubber third T20I at Delhi's Arun Jaitley Stadium, having already sealed the series 2-0.

Captain Shreyas Iyer has hinted that Vaibhav Sooryavanshi could finally get his chance after being benched for the first two matches.

Sanju Samson answered his critics with a match-winning 57 off 22 balls in the second T20I.

Will Vaibhav Sooryavanshi finally get his chance against Afghanistan?

India head into the third T20I against Afghanistan on Thursday with nothing left to play for in terms of the series result, and that has opened the door for a selection call that had looked increasingly unlikely just two days ago.

Sanju Samson silenced any lingering doubts about his place in the second T20I, striking a 22-ball 57, his biggest score since the T20 World Cup, to help India chase down 160 in just 14.5 overs and wrap up the series with a match to spare.

That knock came after a low score of 10 from the opener, which had put his position under scrutiny, with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi still waiting for a game. Despite Samson's response, captain Shreyas Iyer used his post-match press conference to signal that changes are coming for the dead rubber.

Speaking after the win, Iyer stressed the value of giving fringe squad members game time and familiarity with conditions, a comment widely read as confirmation that Sooryavanshi could finally make his home debut.

Varun Chakravarthy remains unavailable with the side strain sustained in the opener. That leaves India managing a similar bowling reshuffle to the one that saw Ravi Bishnoi come into the XI for the second match.

India's probable XI and starting lineup for 3rd T20I against Afghanistan

Below is a predicted lineup for India's third and final match of the T20I series against Afghanistan in Delhi.

Afghanistan predicted XI for the Delhi finale

Afghanistan will again lean on their spin-heavy attack led by Rashid Khan, who claimed 3 for 36 in the second match, while looking for their batters to finally get a start against an Indian attack that has bowled them out inside their full quota in both games so far.

Sooryavanshi's chance may have arrived at the wrong moment for Samson

There is a genuine irony in how this selection debate has played out. Samson did exactly what was asked of him after a shaky start, playing the kind of innings that should end any talk of his place being under threat.

Instead, it only led to the series being sealed early, opening the door for the very player he was supposedly holding back. While not a knock on Iyer's thinking, a dead rubber series finale isn't a game where Sooryavanshi can prove his claim for the opener spot.

What it'll do, however, is give the 15-year-old his first look on home soil, particularly with the Asian Games squad needing further clarity before India travel to Japan. The awkward part is what it says about Samson's situation going forward and his position in India's white-ball pecking order.
